prompt: In an election, each voter ranks all candidates from most to least preferred. The *Borda score* of a candidate $c$ for a voter $v$ is the rank $r_v(c)$ of $c$ in $v$'s ranking ($1$ for the most preferred), and the Borda score of $c$ is its average rank over all voters. The candidate with the smallest Borda score wins; ties are broken arbitrarily (you cannot break ties in your favour). There are three voters and three candidates Xavier, Yisa and Zack, whose rankings are: Alice: Xavier $>$ Yisa $>$ Zack, Bob: Zack $>$ Xavier $>$ Yisa, Cady: Yisa $>$ Xavier $>$ Zack (for instance Alice prefers Xavier the most and Zack the least). The Borda score of Zack is $\frac{1+3+3}{3}=\frac73$. Compute the Borda scores of Xavier and Yisa, and explain why Xavier wins.
answer: Xavier $\frac53$, Yisa $2$; Xavier has the smallest score.

solutions.title: Compute
solutions.body: Xavier's ranks are $1$ (Alice), $2$ (Bob), $2$ (Cady): $\frac{1+2+2}3=\frac53$. Yisa's ranks are $2,3,1$: $\frac{2+3+1}3=2$. Zack's score is $\frac73$. Since $\frac53<2<\frac73$, Xavier has the smallest Borda score and wins. ∎

The *Borda score* of a candidate $c$ for a voter $v$ is the rank $r_v(c)$ of $c$ in $v$'s ranking ($1$ for the most preferred), and the Borda score of $c$ is its average rank over all voters. Suppose one more voter is added. Is it possible for Yisa to win? Prove your answer.

solutions.title: Example
solutions.body: Yes. Let the fourth voter rank Yisa $>$ Zack $>$ Xavier. The Borda scores become: Xavier $\frac{1+2+2+3}4=2$, Yisa $\frac{2+3+1+1}4=\frac74$, Zack $\frac{3+1+3+2}4=\frac94$. Yisa has the smallest score and wins. ∎

prompt: In an election, each voter ranks all candidates from most to least preferred. The *Borda score* of a candidate $c$ for a voter $v$ is the rank $r_v(c)$ of $c$ in $v$'s ranking ($1$ for the most preferred), and the Borda score of $c$ is its average rank over all voters. The candidate with the smallest Borda score wins; ties are broken arbitrarily (you cannot break ties in your favour). Suppose a candidate $c$ is ranked first by more than half of the voters. Does $c$ necessarily win under Borda score? Prove your answer.

solutions.title: Counterexample
solutions.body: No. Take the election with five voters and four candidates: $v_1,v_2,v_3$: $c_1>c_2>c_3>c_4$; $v_4,v_5$: $c_4>c_2>c_3>c_1$. Then $c_1$ is ranked first by $3$ of $5$ voters, but the Borda scores are $c_1:\frac{1+1+1+4+4}5=\frac{11}5$, $c_2:2$, $c_3:3$, $c_4:\frac{4+4+4+1+1}5=\frac{14}5$. So $c_2$ wins, not $c_1$. ∎

prompt: In an election, each voter ranks all candidates from most to least preferred. The *Borda score* of a candidate $c$ for a voter $v$ is the rank $r_v(c)$ of $c$ in $v$'s ranking ($1$ for the most preferred), and the Borda score of $c$ is its average rank over all voters. The candidate with the smallest Borda score wins; ties are broken arbitrarily (you cannot break ties in your favour). Suppose $c$ wins under Borda score in an election. We improve the position of $c$ in some of the votes and leave everything else the same (i.e. if we exclude $c$, the rankings are the same as before the change). Does $c$ still win? Prove your answer.

solutions.title: Scores move the right way
solutions.body: Yes. Improving $c$'s position in a vote strictly decreases $r_v(c)$, so the Borda score of $c$ decreases. Every other candidate's rank in that vote either stays the same or increases by $1$ (a candidate passed by $c$ moves down one place), so their Borda scores do not decrease. Hence $c$ still has the smallest Borda score. ∎

prompt: In an election, each voter ranks all candidates from most to least preferred. The *Borda score* of a candidate $c$ for a voter $v$ is the rank $r_v(c)$ of $c$ in $v$'s ranking ($1$ for the most preferred), and the Borda score of $c$ is its average rank over all voters. The candidate with the smallest Borda score wins; ties are broken arbitrarily (you cannot break ties in your favour). Suppose $c$ wins under Borda score in an election. We then change the votes in such a way that, for each vote, every candidate $w$ who was ranked below $c$ originally is still ranked below $c$ in the new vote. Does $c$ necessarily still win under the new votes? Prove your answer.

solutions.title: Counterexample
solutions.body: No. Use the election from 2(a): $v_1,v_2,v_3$: $c_1>c_2>c_3>c_4$; $v_4,v_5$: $c_4>c_2>c_3>c_1$, where $c_2$ wins with Borda score $2$. Change the votes of $v_4$ and $v_5$ to $c_4>c_2>c_1>c_3$. Candidates ranked below $c_2$ in a vote of $v_4,v_5$ were $c_3,c_1$, and they are still below $c_2$; the other votes are unchanged. Now the scores are $c_1:\frac{1+1+1+3+3}5=\frac95$, $c_2:2$, $c_3:\frac{3+3+3+4+4}5=\frac{17}5$, $c_4:\frac{14}5$. So $c_1$ wins and $c_2$ no longer does. ∎

prompt: There are $n$ voters and $m$ candidates; $r_v(c)$ is the rank of candidate $c$ for voter $v$ ($1$ is the best). A *committee* is a set $T$ of candidates. Its Borda score for voter $v$ is $r_v(T)=\min_{c\in T}r_v(c)$, and its Borda score is $r_{\mathcal V}(T)=\frac1n\sum_vr_v(T)$ (the average over voters of the best rank in the committee). Consider the election with five voters $v_1,\dots,v_5$ and five candidates $c_1,\dots,c_5$ with preferences $v_1:c_1>c_2>c_3>c_4>c_5$, $v_2:c_2>c_1>c_4>c_3>c_5$, $v_3:c_5>c_2>c_1>c_3>c_4$, $v_4:c_3>c_4>c_2>c_5>c_1$, $v_5:c_4>c_1>c_2>c_3>c_5$. Find the committee of size $2$ with the smallest Borda score, and compute its Borda score.

solutions.title: Check all committees
solutions.body: The committee $\{c_2,c_4\}$ gives best ranks $2,1,2,2,1$ for $v_1,\dots,v_5$ (ranks of $c_2$: $2,1,2,3,3$ and of $c_4$: $4,3,5,2,1$), so its score is $\frac{2+1+2+2+1}5=\frac85$. Checking all $\binom52=10$ committees, every other committee has a larger score: the next best are $\{c_1,c_2\}$ and $\{c_1,c_3\}$ with score $\frac95$. So the answer is $\{c_2,c_4\}$ with score $\frac85$.

prompt: There are $n$ voters and $m$ candidates; $r_v(c)$ is the rank of candidate $c$ for voter $v$ ($1$ is the best). A *committee* is a set $T$ of candidates. Its Borda score for voter $v$ is $r_v(T)=\min_{c\in T}r_v(c)$, and its Borda score is $r_{\mathcal V}(T)=\frac1n\sum_vr_v(T)$ (the average over voters of the best rank in the committee). Given an election, let $T^*_k$ denote a committee of size $k$ with the smallest Borda score. Is it necessarily true that $T^*_k\subset T^*_{k+1}$? Prove your answer.

solutions.title: Counterexample
solutions.body: No. Use the election of 2(a): $v_1,v_2,v_3:c_1>c_2>c_3>c_4$; $v_4,v_5:c_4>c_2>c_3>c_1$. The single candidates have scores $c_1:\frac{11}5$, $c_2:2$, $c_3:3$, $c_4:\frac{14}5$, so $T_1^*=\{c_2\}$. The committee $\{c_1,c_4\}$ has score $1$ (every voter has $c_1$ or $c_4$ in first place), which is the minimum possible, and a score of $1$ requires the committee to contain both first choices $c_1$ and $c_4$. So $T_2^*=\{c_1,c_4\}\not\supset\{c_2\}=T_1^*$. ∎

prompt: There are $n$ voters and $m$ candidates; $r_v(c)$ is the rank of candidate $c$ for voter $v$ ($1$ is the best). A *committee* is a set $T$ of candidates. Its Borda score for voter $v$ is $r_v(T)=\min_{c\in T}r_v(c)$, and its Borda score is $r_{\mathcal V}(T)=\frac1n\sum_vr_v(T)$ (the average over voters of the best rank in the committee). Suppose we select $k$ candidates uniformly at random (among all $\binom mk$ subsets of the $m$ candidates) to form a committee $T$. What is the expected value $\mathbf E[r_{\mathcal V}(T)]$ of the Borda score of $T$? Express your answer in terms of $n,m,k$ and prove it.

solutions.title: Expected minimum of a random subset
solutions.body:
By linearity of expectation it suffices to compute the expected best rank for one voter $v$. Since $T$ is a uniformly random $k$-subset of the candidates, the set of ranks $\{r_v(c):c\in T\}$ is a uniformly random $k$-subset $K$ of $\{1,\dots,m\}$, and $r_v(T)=\min K$. For $t\ge1$, $P(\min K\ge t)=\binom{m-t+1}k/\binom mk$, so
$$\mathbf E[\min K]=\sum_{t=1}^mP(\min K\ge t)=\frac{1}{\binom mk}\sum_{t=1}^m\binom{m-t+1}{k}=\frac{\binom{m+1}{k+1}}{\binom mk}=\frac{m+1}{k+1},$$
using the hockey-stick identity $\sum_{j=1}^m\binom jk=\binom{m+1}{k+1}$. This is the same for every voter, so the average over voters is $\frac{m+1}{k+1}$, independent of $n$. ∎

solutions.title: Gaps on a circle
solutions.body: Put $m+1$ points on a circle (the $m$ ranks and one extra point $0$) and choose a uniformly random set of $k+1$ of them, then a uniformly random one $P$ of these $k+1$ points as origin. After rotating so $P=0$, the other $k$ points form a uniformly random $k$-subset of $\{1,\dots,m\}$. The $k+1$ gaps between consecutive chosen points sum to $m+1$, and since the origin is a uniformly random chosen point, all gaps have the same expectation, $\frac{m+1}{k+1}$. The smallest rank in the subset is the first gap from the origin, so $\mathbf E[\min K]=\frac{m+1}{k+1}$. ∎

prompt: There are $n$ voters and $m$ candidates; $r_v(c)$ is the rank of candidate $c$ for voter $v$ ($1$ is the best). A *committee* is a set $T$ of candidates. Its Borda score for voter $v$ is $r_v(T)=\min_{c\in T}r_v(c)$, and its Borda score is $r_{\mathcal V}(T)=\frac1n\sum_vr_v(T)$ (the average over voters of the best rank in the committee). Build committees $\emptyset=T_0\subsetneq T_1\subsetneq\dots\subsetneq T_k$ greedily: in round $j$, pick the candidate $c_j\notin T_{j-1}$ that minimizes $r_{\mathcal V}(T_{j-1}\cup\{c_j\})$ (ties broken arbitrarily); call this procedure Greedy. Consider the election with five voters $v_1,\dots,v_5$ and five candidates $c_1,\dots,c_5$ with preferences $v_1:c_1>c_2>c_3>c_4>c_5$, $v_2:c_2>c_1>c_4>c_3>c_5$, $v_3:c_5>c_2>c_1>c_3>c_4$, $v_4:c_3>c_4>c_2>c_5>c_1$, $v_5:c_4>c_1>c_2>c_3>c_5$. For $k=3$, compute the committee that Greedy produces.
answer: $\{c_1,c_2,c_4\}$ (one of several tied choices in the last round: $\{c_2,c_4,c_1\}$, $\{c_2,c_4,c_3\}$, $\{c_2,c_4,c_5\}$ all have score $\frac75$).

solutions.title: Run Greedy
solutions.body: Round $1$: the single-candidate scores are $c_2:\frac{11}5$ (smallest), $c_1:\frac{13}5$, $c_4:3$, ... so $c_2$ is chosen. Round $2$: adding $c_4$ gives $\frac85$, the smallest ($c_1$ and $c_3$ give $\frac95$). Round $3$: adding any of $c_1,c_3,c_5$ gives the same Borda score $\frac75$ (and $c_1$ is one of the tied best choices). With $c_1$ chosen, Greedy produces $\{c_1,c_2,c_4\}$. ∎

reviewNote: In round 3, c1, c3 and c5 tie (score 7/5), so Greedy's committee depends on tie-breaking; the official answer {c1,c2,c4} is one valid outcome.

prompt: There are $n$ voters and $m$ candidates; $r_v(c)$ is the rank of candidate $c$ for voter $v$ ($1$ is the best). A *committee* is a set $T$ of candidates. Its Borda score for voter $v$ is $r_v(T)=\min_{c\in T}r_v(c)$, and its Borda score is $r_{\mathcal V}(T)=\frac1n\sum_vr_v(T)$ (the average over voters of the best rank in the committee). Build committees $\emptyset=T_0\subsetneq T_1\subsetneq\dots\subsetneq T_k$ greedily: in round $j$, pick the candidate $c_j\notin T_{j-1}$ that minimizes $r_{\mathcal V}(T_{j-1}\cup\{c_j\})$ (ties broken arbitrarily); call this procedure Greedy. Does Greedy always produce an optimal committee, i.e. one with the smallest Borda score? Prove your answer.

solutions.title: Counterexample
solutions.body: No. Take the election of 2(a): $v_1,v_2,v_3:c_1>c_2>c_3>c_4$; $v_4,v_5:c_4>c_2>c_3>c_1$. The best committee of size $2$ is $\{c_1,c_4\}$ with score $1$. Greedy first picks $c_2$ (score $2$, the smallest single score), and then adding $c_1$ gives $\frac{1+1+1+2+2}5=\frac75$, adding $c_4$ gives $\frac{2+2+2+1+1}5=\frac85$, adding $c_3$ gives $2$. So Greedy produces $\{c_1,c_2\}$ with score $\frac75>1$. ∎

There are $n$ voters and $m$ candidates; $r_v(c)$ is the rank of candidate $c$ for voter $v$ ($1$ is the best). A *committee* is a set $T$ of candidates. Its Borda score for voter $v$ is $r_v(T)=\min_{c\in T}r_v(c)$, and its Borda score is $r_{\mathcal V}(T)=\frac1n\sum_vr_v(T)$ (the average over voters of the best rank in the committee). Let $T_j$ be the committee after $j$ rounds ($1\le j<m$) and write $r_v(T_j)$ and $r_{\mathcal V}(T_j)$ for its Borda scores. Prove that
$$r_{\mathcal V}(T_j)-r_{\mathcal V}(T_{j+1})\ \ge\ \frac{\sum_{v\in\mathcal V}r_v(T_j)\,(r_v(T_j)-1)}{2n(m-j)}.$$

prompt:
There are $n$ voters and $m$ candidates; $r_v(c)$ is the rank of candidate $c$ for voter $v$ ($1$ is the best). A *committee* is a set $T$ of candidates. Its Borda score for voter $v$ is $r_v(T)=\min_{c\in T}r_v(c)$, and its Borda score is $r_{\mathcal V}(T)=\frac1n\sum_vr_v(T)$ (the average over voters of the best rank in the committee). Build committees $\emptyset=T_0\subsetneq T_1\subsetneq\dots\subsetneq T_k$ greedily: in round $j$, pick the candidate $c_j\notin T_{j-1}$ that minimizes $r_{\mathcal V}(T_{j-1}\cup\{c_j\})$ (ties broken arbitrarily); call this procedure Greedy. Let $\mathrm{Rand}(k)=\frac{m+1}{k+1}$ be the expected Borda score of a random committee of size $k$ (Problem 3(c)). You may use the following inequality (Problem 4(c)): for $1\le j<m$, $r_{\mathcal V}(T_j)-r_{\mathcal V}(T_{j+1})\ge\frac{\sum_{v}r_v(T_j)(r_v(T_j)-1)}{2n(m-j)}$. Show that for every election and every $k\ge1$,
$$r_{\mathcal V}(T_k)\le2\cdot\mathrm{Rand}(k).$$

solutions.title: Induction using 4(c) and Cauchy-Schwarz
solutions.body:
Write $\bar r_j=r_{\mathcal V}(T_j)$. We prove $\bar r_k\le\frac{2(m+1)}{k+1}$ by induction on $k$.

**Base case $k=1$.** Greedy picks the candidate of smallest Borda score, which is at most the average Borda score $\frac{m+1}2$, so $\bar r_1\le\frac{m+1}2\le m+1$.

**Step.** Let $k\ge2$ and assume $\bar r_{k-1}\le\frac{2(m+1)}k$. If $\bar r_{k-1}\le\frac{2(m+1)}{k+1}$ we are done since scores do not increase ($\bar r_k\le\bar r_{k-1}$). So assume
$$\frac{2(m+1)}{k+1}<\bar r_{k-1}\le\frac{2(m+1)}{k}.$$
Let $\rho_v=r_v(T_{k-1})$, so $\sum_v\rho_v=n\bar r_{k-1}$. By Cauchy-Schwarz $\sum_v\rho_v^2\ge\frac1n\left(\sum_v\rho_v\right)^2=n\bar r_{k-1}^2$. By 4(c) with $j=k-1$,
$$\bar r_{k-1}-\bar r_k\ge\frac{\sum_v\rho_v^2-\sum_v\rho_v}{2n(m-k+1)}\ge\frac{n\bar r_{k-1}^2-n\bar r_{k-1}}{2n(m-k+1)}=\frac{\bar r_{k-1}^2}{2(m-k+1)}\left(1-\frac1{\bar r_{k-1}}\right).$$
Since $\bar r_{k-1}>\frac{2(m+1)}{k+1}$, we have $1-\frac1{\bar r_{k-1}}>1-\frac{k+1}{2(m+1)}=\frac{2m+1-k}{2(m+1)}$, so
$$\bar r_{k-1}-\bar r_k\ge\bar r_{k-1}^2\cdot\frac{2m+1-k}{4(m+1)(m-k+1)}\ge\frac{\bar r_{k-1}^2}{2(m+1)},$$
because $\frac{2m+1-k}{2(m-k+1)}\ge1\iff k\ge1$. Therefore
$$\bar r_k\le f(\bar r_{k-1}),\qquad f(t)=t-\frac{t^2}{2(m+1)}.$$
The function $f$ is increasing for $t\le m+1$, and $\bar r_{k-1}\le\frac{2(m+1)}k\le m+1$, so
$$\bar r_k\le f\!\left(\frac{2(m+1)}k\right)=\frac{2(m+1)}k-\frac{2(m+1)}{k^2}=\frac{2(m+1)(k-1)}{k^2}\le\frac{2(m+1)}{k+1},$$
since $(k-1)(k+1)\le k^2$. This completes the induction, and $\frac{2(m+1)}{k+1}=2\,\mathrm{Rand}(k)$. ∎

prompt: There are $n$ voters and $m$ candidates; $r_v(c)$ is the rank of candidate $c$ for voter $v$ ($1$ is the best). A *committee* is a set $T$ of candidates. Its Borda score for voter $v$ is $r_v(T)=\min_{c\in T}r_v(c)$, and its Borda score is $r_{\mathcal V}(T)=\frac1n\sum_vr_v(T)$ (the average over voters of the best rank in the committee). Build committees $\emptyset=T_0\subsetneq T_1\subsetneq\dots\subsetneq T_k$ greedily: in round $j$, pick the candidate $c_j\notin T_{j-1}$ that minimizes $r_{\mathcal V}(T_{j-1}\cup\{c_j\})$ (ties broken arbitrarily); call this procedure Greedy. Let $\mathrm{Rand}(k)=\frac{m+1}{k+1}$. Show that there exists an election for which $r_{\mathcal V}(T_k)>\mathrm{Rand}(k)$ (for some $k$).

solutions.title: A construction
solutions.body:
Take an even $m\ge6$, $k=2$, and $n=(m-1)!$ voters: candidate $c_1$ is ranked in position $\frac m2$ by every voter, and the other $m-1$ candidates fill the remaining positions in every possible order (each of the $(m-1)!$ orders appears exactly once).

**Round 1.** For $c\ne c_1$ the position of $c$ among the $m-1$ other candidates is uniform in $\{1,\dots,m-1\}$ and its true rank is $\rho$ if $\rho<\frac m2$ and $\rho+1$ otherwise. Its average rank is
$$\frac{1}{m-1}\left[\sum_{\rho=1}^{m/2-1}\rho+\sum_{\rho=m/2}^{m-1}(\rho+1)\right]=\frac{m^2}{2(m-1)}>\frac m2,$$
which is larger than $c_1$'s score $\frac m2$. So Greedy picks $c_1$.

**Round 2.** Adding any $c\ne c_1$ (all equivalent by symmetry) gives the average of $\min(\frac m2,\mathrm{rank}(c))$, which equals
$$\frac1{m-1}\left[\sum_{\rho=1}^{m/2-1}\rho+\frac m2\cdot\frac m2\right]=\frac{m(3m-2)}{8(m-1)}.$$
So $r_{\mathcal V}(T_2)=\frac{m(3m-2)}{8(m-1)}$, while $\mathrm{Rand}(2)=\frac{m+1}3$. We have $\frac{m(3m-2)}{8(m-1)}>\frac{m+1}3\iff9m^2-6m>8m^2-8\iff(m-2)(m-4)>0$, true for $m\ge6$. For example $m=6$ (with $n=120$ voters): $\frac{12}5=2.4>\frac73\approx2.33$. ∎

prompt: There are $n$ voters and $m$ candidates; $r_v(c)$ is the rank of candidate $c$ for voter $v$ ($1$ is the best). A *committee* is a set $T$ of candidates. Its Borda score for voter $v$ is $r_v(T)=\min_{c\in T}r_v(c)$, and its Borda score is $r_{\mathcal V}(T)=\frac1n\sum_vr_v(T)$ (the average over voters of the best rank in the committee). The *$s$-Borda score* of a committee $T$ is $r_{\mathcal V}(T)=\frac1n\sum_{v\in\mathcal V}\left(\min_{Q\subseteq T,\ |Q|=s}\sum_{c\in Q}r_v(c)\right)$. Interpret this definition in plain English.
answer: For each voter take the $s$ best-ranked committee members, add their ranks; then average over voters.

solutions.title: Plain English
solutions.body: For each voter, look at the $s$ members of the committee that this voter ranks highest (smallest ranks) and add up their ranks; this is the minimum over all $s$-element subsets $Q$ of the committee. The $s$-Borda score is the average of this number over all voters. (For $s=1$ it is the ordinary committee Borda score.)

prompt: There are $n$ voters and $m$ candidates; $r_v(c)$ is the rank of candidate $c$ for voter $v$ ($1$ is the best). A *committee* is a set $T$ of candidates. Its Borda score for voter $v$ is $r_v(T)=\min_{c\in T}r_v(c)$, and its Borda score is $r_{\mathcal V}(T)=\frac1n\sum_vr_v(T)$ (the average over voters of the best rank in the committee). The $s$-Borda score of a committee $T$ is $r_{\mathcal V}(T)=\frac1n\sum_{v}\min_{Q\subseteq T,|Q|=s}\sum_{c\in Q}r_v(c)$. In the election with five voters $v_1,\dots,v_5$ and five candidates $c_1,\dots,c_5$ with preferences $v_1:c_1>c_2>c_3>c_4>c_5$, $v_2:c_2>c_1>c_4>c_3>c_5$, $v_3:c_5>c_2>c_1>c_3>c_4$, $v_4:c_3>c_4>c_2>c_5>c_1$, $v_5:c_4>c_1>c_2>c_3>c_5$, take $s=2$ and find the committee of size $3$ with the smallest $s$-Borda score.

solutions.title: Compare all committees
solutions.body: For $T=\{c_1,c_2,c_4\}$ the ranks of $(c_1,c_2,c_4)$ are $v_1:(1,2,4)$, $v_2:(2,1,3)$, $v_3:(3,2,5)$, $v_4:(5,3,2)$, $v_5:(2,3,1)$. The sum of the two smallest ranks for each voter: $3,3,5,5,3$, total $19$, average $\frac{19}5$. Checking all $\binom53=10$ committees of size $3$, the next best score is $4$ ($\{c_1,c_2,c_3\}$), so $\{c_1,c_2,c_4\}$ is the unique minimizer. ∎

prompt: There are $n$ voters and $m$ candidates; $r_v(c)$ is the rank of candidate $c$ for voter $v$ ($1$ is the best). A *committee* is a set $T$ of candidates. Its Borda score for voter $v$ is $r_v(T)=\min_{c\in T}r_v(c)$, and its Borda score is $r_{\mathcal V}(T)=\frac1n\sum_vr_v(T)$ (the average over voters of the best rank in the committee). The $s$-Borda score of a committee $T$ is $r_{\mathcal V}(T)=\frac1n\sum_{v}\min_{Q\subseteq T,|Q|=s}\sum_{c\in Q}r_v(c)$. If we select $k\ge s$ candidates uniformly at random to form a committee $T$, what is $\mathbf E[r_{\mathcal V}(T)]$? Prove your answer.

solutions.title: Expected sum of the s smallest ranks
solutions.body:
For one voter, the ranks of the committee members form a uniformly random $k$-subset $K$ of $\{1,\dots,m\}$, and the voter's contribution is the sum of the $s$ smallest elements of $K$: $\kappa_1+\dots+\kappa_s$ with $\kappa_1<\kappa_2<\dots$. Put $\kappa_0=0$ and $g_i=\kappa_i-\kappa_{i-1}$ for $i=1,\dots,k$, and $g_{k+1}=m+1-\kappa_k$. These $k+1$ gaps sum to $m+1$ and, by the circle argument of 3(c) (choose a random $(k+1)$-subset of $m+1$ points on a circle and a random one of them as origin), all have the same expectation $\frac{m+1}{k+1}$. Hence $\mathbf E[\kappa_i]=\mathbf E[g_1+\dots+g_i]=i\frac{m+1}{k+1}$, and
$$\mathbf E\left[\sum_{i=1}^s\kappa_i\right]=\frac{m+1}{k+1}\sum_{i=1}^si=\frac{s(s+1)}2\cdot\frac{m+1}{k+1}.$$
This holds for every voter, so the average over voters has the same expectation. ∎
